sections.title: The True Petition of the Sangam of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam

tamil: 4. சமரச சுத்த சன்மார்க்க சங்க சத்திய விண்ணப்பம்
திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்
translit: 4. camaraca cutta caṉmārkka caṅka cattiya viṇṇappam
tirucciṟṟampalam
translation: The True Petition of the Sangam of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam. Tiruchitrambalam.
commentary: The title calls this work a viṇṇappam, a petition laid before God, and calls it true (cattiya). It is the petition of the caṅkam, the Sangam: the fellowship of those who walk Vallalar's path of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam, the Universal Pure True Path. The name stands within the petition itself, at the end of its opening address (§2). The editions did not always keep it: some placed this petition first and called it a small petition, and in the copies made by his devotees it is not numbered with the other three. Here it stands fourth, as in the later printed editions. It is the shortest of the four. Like the Great True Petition and the True Petition of Wisdom, it speaks as "I", addresses God as Tēvarīr, the most reverent word for "You", and opens and closes with Tiruchitrambalam.

sections.title: The Petition Laid Before Arut Perum Jothi at Vadalur

tamil: உத்தர ஞான சித்திபுரம் என்றும் உத்தர ஞான சிதம்பரம் என்றும் திருவருளால் ஆக்கப்பட்ட ஆக்கச் சிறப்புப் பெயர்களும், பார்வதிபுரம் என்றும் வடலூர் என்றும் உலகியலாற் குறிக்கப்பட்ட குறிப்புப் பெயர்களும் பெற்று விளங்குகின்ற தெய்வப் பதியினிடத்தே, இயற்கை விளக்க நிறைவாகியுள்ள ஒரு சுத்த சிவானுபவ ஞானசபையில், இயற்கை உண்மை நிறைவாகிய திருவுருவைத் தரித்து, இயற்கை இன்ப நிறைவாகிய சிவானந்த ஒருமைத் திருநடச் செய்கையை எவ்வுயிரும் இன்பமடைதற் பொருட்டே செய்தருளுகின்ற எல்லாம் வல்ல தனித்தலைமைக் கடவுளாகிய அருட்பெருஞ்ஜோதி ஆண்டவரே! தேவரீரது திருவருட் சமுகத்தில் யான் செய்து கொள்ளுகின்ற சமரச சுத்த சன்மார்க்க சங்க சத்திய விண்ணப்பம்.
translit: uttara ñāṉa cittipuram eṉṟum uttara ñāṉa citamparam eṉṟum tiruvaruḷāl ākkappaṭṭa ākkac ciṟappup peyarkaḷum, pārvatipuram eṉṟum vaṭalūr eṉṟum ulakiyalāṟ kuṟikkappaṭṭa kuṟippup peyarkaḷum peṟṟu viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvap patiyiṉiṭattē, iyaṟkai viḷakka niṟaivākiyuḷḷa oru cutta civāṉupava ñāṉacapaiyil, iyaṟkai uṇmai niṟaivākiya tiruvuruvait tarittu, iyaṟkai iṉpa niṟaivākiya civāṉanta orumait tirunaṭac ceykaiyai evvuyirum iṉpamaṭaitaṟ poruṭṭē ceytaruḷukiṉṟa ellām valla taṉittalaimaik kaṭavuḷākiya aruṭperuñjōti āṇṭavarē! tēvarīratu tiruvaruṭ camukattil yāṉ ceytu koḷḷukiṉṟa camaraca cutta caṉmārkka caṅka cattiya viṇṇappam.
translation: O Lord Arut Perum Jothi, God of unique supremacy, the All-Powerful! There is a divine place that bears the names of honour made by holy grace, Uttara Jnana Siddhipuram and Uttara Jnana Chidambaram, and the names by which the world marks it, Parvatipuram and Vadalur. There, in a pure Hall of Wisdom of Siva-experience, filled with natural illumination, You bear a holy form full of natural truth, and You perform the holy dance of the oneness of Siva-bliss, full of natural bliss, only so that every living being may attain bliss. In the holy presence of Your grace I make this, the true petition of the Sangam of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam.
commentary: The opening follows the invocation of the Great True Petition (Peru §2) almost word for word. God is named by three things that belong to His own nature: natural illumination fills the place, natural truth is His holy form, natural bliss is His holy dance. That dance has one purpose: that every living being may attain bliss. Two things are new here. The place is named: Vadalur, which the world also calls Parvatipuram, and which grace has named Uttara Jnana Siddhipuram and Uttara Jnana Chidambaram. And where Peru speaks of a Space of Siva-experience, here it is a Hall of Wisdom (ñāṉacapai), the Sathya Jnana Sabha at Vadalur. The printed editions read "filled with natural illumination"; the online text repeats "natural truth" here. Vallalar makes his petition in the holy presence of God's grace (tiruvaruṭ camukam).

sections.title: The One Desire: An Eternal Body

tamil: இவ்வுலகினிடத்து ஆறறிவுள்ள உயர்வுடைத்தாகிய தேகத்தைப் பெற்ற யான் இத் தேகத்திற்கு இடைக்கிடை நேருகின்ற மரணம், பிணி, மூப்பு, பயம், துன்ப முதலிய அவத்தைகள் எல்லாவற்றையும் நிவர்த்தி செய்து, இத் தேகத்தையே நித்திய தேகமாக்கிக்கொண்டு எக்காலத்தும் எவ்விடத்தும் எவ்விதத்தும் எத்துணையும் தடைபடாத பேரின்ப சித்திப் பெருவாழ்வைப் பெற்று வாழ்தல் வேண்டும் என்பதே எனது சத்தியமான அதிதீவிர விருப்ப முயற்சியாக இருக்கின்றது.
translit: ivvulakiṉiṭattu āṟaṟivuḷḷa uyarvuṭaittākiya tēkattaip peṟṟa yāṉ it tēkattiṟku iṭaikkiṭai nērukiṉṟa maraṇam, piṇi, mūppu, payam, tuṉpa mutaliya avattaikaḷ ellāvaṟṟaiyum nivartti ceytu, it tēkattaiyē nittiya tēkamākkikkoṇṭu ekkālattum evviṭattum evvitattum ettuṇaiyum taṭaipaṭāta pēriṉpa cittip peruvāḻvaip peṟṟu vāḻtal vēṇṭum eṉpatē eṉatu cattiyamāṉa atitīvira viruppa muyaṟciyāka irukkiṉṟatu.
translation: In this world I have received a body of high standing, which has six kinds of awareness. Death, disease, old age, fear, suffering and the other afflictions come upon this body from time to time. To remove them all, to make this very body an eternal body, and to attain and live the great life that is the attainment of supreme bliss, hindered at no time, in no place, in no way and to no degree: this is my true desire and my most intense endeavour.
commentary: Vallalar says plainly what he asks for. He does not ask to leave the body, or to be released from it at death. He asks that this very body (it tēkattaiyē) be made an eternal body (nittiya tēkam), free of death, disease, old age, fear and suffering. The Small True Petition names the same afflictions and the same great life (Siru §13), and the Great True Petition calls this body the highest of all bodies, with six kinds of awareness (Peru §2). He calls it his true desire and his most intense endeavour (atitīvira virupa muyaṟci): the aim of all his effort.

sections.title: Grace Alone Can Give It

tamil: எனது விருப்ப முயற்சி இங்ஙனமாக, அவத்தைகள் எல்லாவற்றையும் நீக்கி இத்தேகத்தை நித்திய தேகமாக்கி எக்காலத்தும் அழியாத பேரின்ப சித்திப் பெருவாழ்வைப் பெற்று வாழ்தல் எதனால் பெறுதல் கூடுமென்று அறியத் தொடங்கிய தருணத்து, வேறு எந்த வழியாலும் பெறுதல் கூடாது, எல்லாமுடைய கடவுளது திருவருட் சுதந்தரம் ஒன்றாலே பெறுதல் கூடுமென்று தேவரீர் திருவருளால் அறிவிக்க உள்ளபடி அறிந்தேன்.
translit: eṉatu viruppa muyaṟci iṅṅaṉamāka, avattaikaḷ ellāvaṟṟaiyum nīkki ittēkattai nittiya tēkamākki ekkālattum aḻiyāta pēriṉpa cittip peruvāḻvaip peṟṟu vāḻtal etaṉāl peṟutal kūṭumeṉṟu aṟiyat toṭaṅkiya taruṇattu, vēṟu enta vaḻiyālum peṟutal kūṭātu, ellāmuṭaiya kaṭavuḷatu tiruvaruṭ cutantaram oṉṟālē peṟutal kūṭumeṉṟu tēvarīr tiruvaruḷāl aṟivikka uḷḷapaṭi aṟintēṉ.
translation: Such being my desire and endeavour, I began to ask by what means one could remove all the afflictions, make this body an eternal body, and attain and live the great life that is the attainment of supreme bliss, which never perishes. Then, as Your holy grace made it known, I knew truly: it cannot be attained by any other way; it can be attained only by the freedom of the holy grace of God, who possesses all.
commentary: Now the question is how. The answer comes from grace itself: by no other way, only by the freedom of grace (tiruvaruṭ cutantaram). Cutantaram means freedom: the power to act by one's own right. Here the freedom is God's. The deathless life cannot be won by effort, practice or merit; grace gives it, acting freely. Vallalar does not say he found this out. He says grace made it known (aṟivikka), and he knew it as it is.

sections.title: The Three Freedoms

tamil: பின்னர், திருவருட் சுதந்தரம் நமக்கு எந்த வழியால் கிடைக்கும் என்று அறியத் தொடங்கிய தருணத்து, எனது யான் என்னும் தேக சுதந்தரம், போக சுதந்தரம், ஜீவ சுதந்தரம் என்னும் மூவகைச் சுதந்தரங்களும் நீங்கியவிடத்தே கிடைக்கும் என்று தேவரீர் திருவருளால் அறிவிக்க உள்ளபடி அறிந்தேன்.
translit: piṉṉar, tiruvaruṭ cutantaram namakku enta vaḻiyāl kiṭaikkum eṉṟu aṟiyat toṭaṅkiya taruṇattu, eṉatu yāṉ eṉṉum tēka cutantaram, pōka cutantaram, jīva cutantaram eṉṉum mūvakaic cutantaraṅkaḷum nīṅkiyaviṭattē kiṭaikkum eṉṟu tēvarīr tiruvaruḷāl aṟivikka uḷḷapaṭi aṟintēṉ.
translation: Then I began to ask by what way the freedom of holy grace would come to us. As Your holy grace made it known, I knew truly: it comes where the three kinds of freedom that make up my "I" have gone: the freedom of the body, the freedom of enjoyment and the freedom of the soul.
commentary: Here the petition turns. The freedom of grace comes only where our own freedoms have gone. Vallalar names three, and together he calls them "my I" (eṉatu yāṉ). The freedom of the body (tēka cutantaram) is the claim that the body is ours to rule. The freedom of enjoyment (pōka cutantaram) is the claim over what the body receives and enjoys. The freedom of the soul (jīva cutantaram) is the claim that life itself is our own. He asks how grace comes "to us" (namakku): what he learns, he learns for all.

sections.title: The Gift of All Three Freedoms to Grace

tamil: ஆகலில், எனது சுதந்தரமாகக் கொண்டிருந்த தேக சுதந்தரத்தையும், போக சுதந்தரத்தையும், ஜீவ சுதந்தரத்தையும் தேவரீர் திருவருட்கே சர்வ சுதந்தரமாகக் கொடுத்து விட்டேன். கொடுத்த தருணத்தே, இத்தேகமும் ஜீவனும் போகப்பொருள்களும் சர்வ சுதந்தரராகிய கடவுள் பெருங்கருணையாற் கொடுக்கப் பெற்றனம் அன்றி, நமது சுதந்தரத்தாற் பெற்றனவல்ல என்னும் உண்மையை அருளால் அறிவிக்கவும் அறிந்து கொண்டேன். இனி இத்தேகத்தினிடத்தும் ஜீவனிடத்தும் போகப்பொருள்களிடத்தும் தேவரீர் திருவருள் சாட்சியாக எனக்கு எவ்விதத்தும் யாதோர் சுதந்தரத் தோற்றமும் தோற்றமாட்டாது. தேவரீர் திருவருட் சுதந்தரத்தை என்னிடத்தே வைத்தருளி, மரணம், பிணி, மூப்பு, பயம், துன்பம் முதலிய அவத்தைகள் எல்லாவற்றையும் தவிர்த்து, இத்தேகத்தையே நித்திய தேகமாக்கி எக்காலத்தும் அழியாத பேரின்ப சித்திப் பெருவாழ்வில் என்னை வாழ்வித்தல் வேண்டும்.
translit: ākalil, eṉatu cutantaramākak koṇṭirunta tēka cutantarattaiyum, pōka cutantarattaiyum, jīva cutantarattaiyum tēvarīr tiruvaruṭkē carva cutantaramākak koṭuttu viṭṭēṉ. koṭutta taruṇattē, ittēkamum jīvaṉum pōkapporuḷkaḷum carva cutantararākiya kaṭavuḷ peruṅkaruṇaiyāṟ koṭukkap peṟṟaṉam aṉṟi, namatu cutantarattāṟ peṟṟaṉavalla eṉṉum uṇmaiyai aruḷāl aṟivikkavum aṟintu koṇṭēṉ. iṉi ittēkattiṉiṭattum jīvaṉiṭattum pōkapporuḷkaḷiṭattum tēvarīr tiruvaruḷ cāṭciyāka eṉakku evvitattum yātōr cutantarat tōṟṟamum tōṟṟamāṭṭātu. tēvarīr tiruvaruṭ cutantarattai eṉṉiṭattē vaittaruḷi, maraṇam, piṇi, mūppu, payam, tuṉpam mutaliya avattaikaḷ ellāvaṟṟaiyum tavirttu, ittēkattaiyē nittiya tēkamākki ekkālattum aḻiyāta pēriṉpa cittip peruvāḻvil eṉṉai vāḻvittal vēṇṭum.
translation: Therefore I have given the freedom of the body, the freedom of enjoyment and the freedom of the soul, which I held as my own freedom, wholly to Your holy grace, as all freedom. The moment I gave them, grace made known to me, and I came to know, this truth: this body, this soul and the things we enjoy were given to us by the great compassion of God, who alone has all freedom; we did not gain them by our own freedom. From now on, with Your holy grace as witness, no appearance of any freedom of mine will arise in me, in any way, over this body, this soul or the things we enjoy. I pray that You place the freedom of Your holy grace in me, remove death, disease, old age, fear, suffering and all such afflictions, make this very body an eternal body, and make me live in the great life that is the attainment of supreme bliss, which never perishes.
commentary: Vallalar does what grace has shown him. He gives all three freedoms to grace as all freedom (carva cutantaram), keeping nothing back. At the moment of giving he learns a second truth: the body, the soul and the things enjoyed were never won by his own freedom. God's great compassion gave them. What he gives up was never his. So from now on, with grace as witness, no claim of freedom will appear in him over any of them. Only then does he ask again for what he asked at first, the eternal body and the deathless great life, now as one who holds nothing as his own. The sentence on what grace made him know at the moment of giving is missing from the online text; it is given here from the printed editions.

sections.title: For All Living Beings

tamil: இத் தேகத்தைப் பெற்ற எல்லாச் சீவர்களுக்கும் எனக்கு அறிவித்த வண்ணமே அறிவித்து, அவரவர்களையும் உரிமையுடையவர்களாக்கி வாழ்வித்தல் வேண்டும்.
translit: it tēkattaip peṟṟa ellāc cīvarkaḷukkum eṉakku aṟivitta vaṇṇamē aṟivittu, avaravarkaḷaiyum urimaiyuṭaiyavarkaḷākki vāḻvittal vēṇṭum.
translation: To all living beings who have received this body, make it known just as You made it known to me; make each of them, too, a holder of that right, and make them live that life.
commentary: The petition does not end with Vallalar. The deathless life he asks for himself, he asks for every living being who has received this body (it tēkattaip peṟṟa ellāc cīvarkaḷ). The word is urimai, right: what grace gives one, it gives as a right to all, as in the right of oneness in soul-kinship of the Small True Petition (Siru §18). This is why it is the petition of the Sangam: a prayer for all.

sections.title: Salutations to the Reign of Great Compassion

tamil: தேவரீர் பெருங்கருணை ஆட்சிக்கு வந்தனம்! வந்தனம்!
இங்ஙனம்
சிதம்பரம் இராமலிங்கம்
திருச்சிற்றம்பலம்
சமரச சுத்த சன்மார்க்க சங்க சத்திய விண்ணப்பம் முற்றிற்று.
translit: tēvarīr peruṅkaruṇai āṭcikku vantaṉam! vantaṉam!
iṅṅaṉam
citamparam irāmaliṅkam
tirucciṟṟampalam
camaraca cutta caṉmārkka caṅka cattiya viṇṇappam muṟṟiṟṟu.
translation: Salutations, salutations to the reign of Your great compassion! Thus, Chidambaram Ramalingam. Tiruchitrambalam. The True Petition of the Sangam of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam is complete.
commentary: The petition ends with praise. God rules, and His rule is great compassion (peruṅkaruṇai āṭci). Then Vallalar signs it, as a letter is signed: "Thus" (iṅṅaṉam), and his own name, Chidambaram Ramalingam. The printed editions keep this sign-off, and so do three of the copies made by his devotees. Tiruchitrambalam closes the petition, as it opened it (§1).

glossary.def: Custom, observance: the rules of conduct a group keeps. At a young age God made Vallalar know that the false worldly custom (poyyulaka ācāram) called caste custom and life-stage custom (jāti-ācāram, ācirama-ācāram) is false, and kept him from practising it (Peru §22); He kept him from practising the customs of the religions (camayācāram) even a little (Peru §24). Vallalar prays that the customs of the religions, sects and paths, and worldly custom (ulakācāram) such as varna and ashrama, never take hold of our minds (Siru §18). See jāti, varuṇam, āciramam.

Ashrama: the four prescribed stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant), bound to varna. Vallalar names it, with varna, as worldly custom (ulakācāram), and prays that these worldly customs, notions and distinctions never take hold of our minds (Siru §18). God made him know that life-stage custom, with caste custom, is false worldly custom, and kept him from practising it (Peru §22). See ācāram, varuṇam.

The five functions: the cosmic operations by which the worlds are brought forth and run. The ruling lords carry on all the universes through such functions as creation, preservation and the removal of impurity (turicu nīkkal), where the usual list has destruction (Gnana §2); they are the lords of the five functions (aintoḻiṟ karuttar, Gnana §3). The sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam can grant with ease the functions of bringing forth, setting in motion, withdrawing, veiling and making clear all the tattvas and tattvis (Gnana §8).

Inner, outer, inner-outer and outer-outer: the four regions of every living being and every thing, from the innermost to the outermost. God fills them all without any gap (Siru §12; Gnana §7). He fills and shines within and without (akattum puṟattum) all the universes (Peru §20) and all things, such as the universe and the body (Gnana §5). He guarded Vallalar within and without (Peru §12, §13, §18, §25), and in the form of grace abides within us and outside us (Siru §15, §16). In Peru §16 the parts of the body are inner and inner-outer organs, such as the faculties, energies and states, and outer and outer-outer organs, such as skin, nerve, bone, blood and flesh.

The imperishable great life: the deathless life. God placed us in this human body, which has the high intelligence fit for attaining it (Siru §11). The same goal is named the great life that is the attainment of supreme bliss (pēriṉpa cittip peruvāḻvu, Siru §13). See pēriṉpam.

The Stainless One, the Pure One (a-mala, without impurity), a name of God in the invocation (Siru §2). The name signifies a divine nature untouched by any flaw or stain. Compare niṉmalar, the stainless sages (Gnana §7).

Nectar (Skt. amṛta): the sweet, life-giving essence. Whenever the unborn child grew faint from the closeness and heat of the womb, God made a breeze of nectar (amutak kāṟṟu) blow there softly (Peru §8); whenever it fainted from hunger, He had it fed with nectar formed of the elements (pūtakāriya amutam, Peru §9). The nectar of the head and the nectar of the middle (talaiyamutam, iṭaiyamutam) are among the parts of the body (Peru §16).
The One without beginning. It follows ātiyar, the First, in the invocation (Siru §2): God is the origin of all things, and He Himself has no beginning. Both names are true of the one God.
The Many. It is paired with ēkar, the One (Siru §2). God is perfectly one, and this one God lives within every being in the universe; both names are true of Him.

The powers of the soul: the powers (kalai) of the soul's own energy (āṉma catti). In the father's seed these powers had only budded, and God made them come forth and shine, and nurtured them (Peru §3). In the mother's womb they had blossomed, and God nurtured them so that they came forth and shone without withering (Peru §6). The soul's powers grow under God's care stage by stage, as the body does.

The right of oneness in soul-kinship (Anma Neya Orumaipadu Urimai). Āṉmanēyam is soul-kinship, the love of soul for soul; orumaippāṭu is oneness; urimai is right and rightful belonging, so it belongs to every soul by right. Vallalar calls it the chief aim (mukkiya lakṣiyam) of Suddha Sanmarkkam, and asks God to make it fill and shine among us, never departing, at all times and in all places (Siru §18). In Jeevakarunya Ozhukkam he grounds Jeevakarunyam, compassion for all living beings, in this same kinship.

Ignorance: the absence of all knowledge. Vallalar calls it a great darkness of bondage (aññāṉam eṉṉum periya pācāntakāram) where knowledge did not appear even a little; in it he lay for a long time as a tiny atom-soul (ciṟṟaṇuppacu), until God lifted him out and placed him in this human body (Peru §2). In it "we" lay by nature, in the darkness of ignorance, knowing nothing and feeling nothing, until God made a little knowledge arise in us in a physical body; the first births after it were the stationary births (Siru §4, §5). Those in it are aññāṉikaḷ, the opposite of the sages (ñāṉikaḷ).

The universe and the body: aṇṭam is the universe, the cosmos (the macrocosm); piṇṭam is the body (the microcosm). God fills and shines within and without all things, such as the universe and the body (Gnana §5). The sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam can, by a gracious glance of their holy eyes, perform the attainments of the body (piṇṭa citti), of the cosmos, of the outer cosmos and of the cosmos of cosmoses (Gnana §8). See piṇṭam.

Āriyam: Sanskrit. God did not let Vallalar's desire go toward Āriyam and the other such languages, which breed pomp (iṭampam), clamour (āravāram), toil (pirayācam), great concealment (perumaṟaippu) and the wasting of time (pōtupōkku), but made his mind hold to the southern language, Tamil (Peru §21). See teṉmoḻi.

The Wondrous One, a name of God in the invocation (Siru §2). God is called aṟputak kaṭavuḷ, the wondrous God (Siru §18), and Vallalar asks Him, by the illumination of His wondrous grace (aṟputat tiruvaruḷ), to make us all true devotees (Siru §17).

The dance of grace; also tiruvaruḷ naṭam, the holy dance of grace. Through an intimation of His grace, God made known that He will perform the dance of grace in Uttara Jnana Siddhipuram for an immeasurably long time, so that every siddhi shines forth, to free those who have long suffered death and the other afflictions and bring them to the imperishable attainment of supreme bliss; the time is very near, and a Hall of Wisdom is to be its sign (Siru §15). Compare tirunaṭam, the holy dance of the oneness of Siva-bliss (Peru §2).

The form of grace. Taking the form of grace and abiding within us and outside us (eṅkaḷ akattum puṟattum), God caused the holy Hall of Wisdom to arise and shine without any obstacle (Siru §15). In the same form He is asked to let no obstacle arise in the holy service of its adornment, and to bring that service to completion (Siru §16).

The great Space of Grace. Vallalar addresses God as the True Reality (meypporuḷ kaṭavuḷ) who shines without any division (vikaṟpam illātu) in the form of Arut Perum Jothi in the great Space of Grace (Peru §18). Compare the pure Space of Siva-experience (cutta civāṉupava veḷi, Peru §2) and the Pure Space of Wisdom (cutta ñāṉa veḷi, Siru §3).

Arut Perum Jothi, the Supreme Light of Grace: Vallalar's ultimate name for God. God shines in His own form as Arut Perum Jothi (Peru §2), in the great Space of Grace (Peru §18) and in the Pure Space of Wisdom (Siru §3). He made shine in Vallalar the true knowledge that there is only one true God, Arut Perum Jothi, who shines within and without to give bliss to all living beings (Peru §24). He is called Lord Arut Perum Jothi (aruṭperuñjōti āṇṭavar, Siru §12, §16, §19; Gnana §3, §7) and Arut Perum Jothi, the unique great Lord (Gnana §5). The Jothi is God Himself, not a light God owns; it is real and open to every soul.

Supra-causal action: God's action at the level beyond the causal. Within a single moment, by supra-causal action, God separated Vallalar out of the great darkness called bondage (pācam), in which he had lain in a swoon for time beyond measure, and drew him forth in a supra-causal form of primal matter (atikāraṇap pakuti uru, Peru §14). Causal, ultra-subtle and subtle action follow (Peru §15). See kāraṇak kiriyai, pakuti.

The transcendent: what lies beyond (Skt. atīta, gone beyond). God becomes each experience of the attainment of wisdom, from the wisdom of action at its base stage to Samarasa pure wisdom, and in each of them He blends as the transcendent (āṅkāṅku atītamākik kalantum). Becoming all of them, He is one, and as the transcendent beyond the transcendent (atītātītam) He shines alone (Gnana §9).
The First, the Primal One: God as the origin (āti) of all that exists. It is paired with aṉātiyar, the One without beginning, in the invocation (Siru §2).

State, condition (Skt. avasthā), especially an afflicted state. In Siru it is rendered "affliction": the afflictions through which "we" suffered and died in each class of birth (Siru §5–§10), the many afflictions in the womb, in infancy and in boyhood that left us without knowledge (Siru §12), and death, disease, old age, fear, suffering and the other afflictions from which God's grace frees us (Siru §13–§15). In Peru it names the ordeals of birth, such as the blows of the wind of the blood and the pressing of the birth passage (Peru §11), and the states of waking, dreaming and deep sleep (naṉavu, kaṉavu, cuḻutti) and the rest (Peru §16). In Sanga death, disease, old age, fear and suffering are the afflictions Vallalar asks to be freed from in this very body (Sanga §3, §4, §6).

The learning of deathlessness (literally "undying learning"): the knowledge by which one does not die. The southern language, Tamil (teṉmoḻi), which came to Vallalar by the strength of God's grace, makes this learning known with ease (Peru §21). The same word cākā, undying, names the three bodies of the experience of the deathless art (cākāk kalāṉupava tēkaṅkaḷ), which never perish at any time (Peru §25).

Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam, the Universal Pure True Path: Vallalar's full name for his path (caṉmārkkam, the true path; cutta, pure; camaraca, of universal harmony). It opens the titles of three of the petitions (Peru §1; Gnana §1; Sanga §1). Vallalar asks God to set us all in the state of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam (Siru §17). Its sages have full freedom over all the tattvas and tattvis; asked how the holy presence of Grace is, they give no word and remain still (Gnana §8). Within the petitions the shorter name is usual: see cutta caṉmārkkam.

Universal harmony (Skt. sama, equal; rasa, essence): the first word of the full name of Vallalar's path (see camaraca cutta caṉmārkkam). The sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam shine as the True Ones in whom the six ends are one in harmony (caṭānta camaraca cattiyar, Gnana §8), and the attainments in which God is present end with the attainment of Samarasa pure wisdom (camaraca cutta ñāṉa citti, Gnana §9).

Religions, sects (creeds) and paths. God made Vallalar know, exactly as they are, that the religions, Saivism, Vaishnavism and the rest, with their practices, gods and goals, are varieties of attainment within the tattvas, and their scriptures imagined lore of attainment within the tattvas; and that the sects and paths, Vedanta, Siddhanta and the rest, are distinctions of attainment of a slight fraction of the Suddha Sanmarkkam experience. He kept him from practising them (Peru §24). The religions, sects and paths are the chief obstacle (mukkiyat taṭai) to Suddha Sanmarkkam (Siru §18). In the Arut Perum Jothi Agaval he says God made known to him from the beginning that caste, sect and religion are false (cātiyu matamuñ camayamum poyyeṉa).

Sangam: a fellowship, an assembly of those who share one aim. The fourth petition is the true petition of the Sangam of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam (Sanga §1, §2): the fellowship of those who walk Vallalar's path. It asks for every living being what it asks for one (Sanga §7).

Notions and distinctions: the ideas the mind forms and the differences it draws (Skt. saṅkalpa, a settled conception or resolve; vikalpa, a dividing alternative or doubt). Vallalar asks God that two sets of customs (ācāram), notions and distinctions never take hold of our minds, from now on and for all time: those of the religions, sects and paths, the chief obstacle (mukkiyat taṭai) to Suddha Sanmarkkam, and the worldly ones (ulakācāram), such as varna (caste) and ashrama (the stages of life) (Siru §18).

The six ends (Skt. ṣaḍ-anta): Yoganta, Kalanta, Bodhanta, Nadanta, Vedanta and Siddhanta. Their pure holders, the pure Yogantars, Kalantars and the rest, are sages of Suddha Sanmarkkam (Gnana §7); the sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam are the True Ones in whom the six ends are one in harmony (caṭānta camaraca cattiyar, Gnana §8). Vallalar calls the sects and paths bearing these six names distinctions of attainment of a slight fraction of the Suddha Sanmarkkam experience (Peru §24).

Energies or powers (Skt. śakti) and their agents, the beings who wield them. They find the Pure Space of Wisdom, where God shines as Arut Perum Jothi, exceedingly hard to know (Siru §3). They run every kind of tattva by way of cause and effect, yet cannot perceive the power of attainment of the true sages (Gnana §2). Through the higher and lower energies and their agents God moved Vallalar into a form of the elements and into the physical form (Peru §15); they carry out the body's chief actions, such as knowing (Peru §16). The holy presence of Grace is their cause (Gnana §9): they are powers God has made, not God.

The True Hall of Wisdom (Sathya Jnana Sabha). In the opening invocation it is called natural illumination; there God's true holy form is called natural truth, and He performs the true holy dance called natural bliss (Gnana §2). The name is also that of the Hall at Vadalur: God makes known that a Hall of Wisdom must be established in Uttara Jnana Siddhipuram as the sign of His dance of grace (Siru §15). See ñāṉa capai.

True wisdom. In Peru it is a name of God: the God of true wisdom, the goal of Suddha Sanmarkkam (cutta caṉmārkka lakṣiya cattiya ñāṉak kaṭavuḷ, Peru §17), and the God of unique supremacy who is true Wisdom and Bliss (cattiya ñāṉāṉantat taṉittalaimaik kaṭavuḷ, Peru §15). Compare the true wisdom (uṇmai ñāṉam) that knows there is only one God (Peru §25).

The True One, the absolute reality, a name of God in the invocation (Siru §2). Where physical forms constantly change, God remains the single absolute truth, the unchanging foundation of existence. The sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam are called True Ones (cattiyar, Gnana §8). Not to be confused with cāttiyar, those who have attained.

Those who have attained (Skt. sādhya, what is to be attained), as against cātaṉar, those still in the practice (Skt. sādhana) that leads to it. The sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam have attained the complete form of the blissful experience of natural true wisdom (Gnana §8); all who practise and all who have attained have the holy presence of Grace as their cause (Gnana §9). Not to be confused with cattiyar, the True Ones.

The One whose quality is Consciousness (cit). It is paired with nirkkuṇar, the One beyond the three qualities of nature (Siru §2): God is free of the qualities of nature, and His own quality is pure consciousness.

The tiny atom-soul: ciṟṟaṇu, a minute atom; pacu (Skt. paśu), the soul in bondage, bound by pācam. Vallalar says that for a long time he lay dwindled (arukik kiṭanta) as a tiny atom-soul in the great darkness of bondage called ignorance, until God, the inner light within him, lifted him out and placed him in this human body (Peru §2).

Attainment, accomplishment (Skt. siddhi). Vallalar grades by it: the religions, with their practices, gods and goals, are varieties of attainment within the tattvas (tattuva citti vikaṟpaṅkaḷ), their scriptures imagined lore of attainment within the tattvas (tattuva cittik kaṟpaṉaik kalaikaḷ), and the sects and paths distinctions of attainment of a slight fraction of the Suddha Sanmarkkam experience (cutta caṉmārkka aṉupava lēca citti pētaṅkaḷ, Peru §24). The great life of supreme bliss includes the gift of grace by which all attainments are obtained, of action, of yoga, of wisdom and the rest (Peru §25). Vallalar longs for the attainment of supreme bliss (pēriṉpa citti, Siru §13–§15). No one can grasp the power of attainment (citti vallapam) of the true sages (Gnana §2).

The play of Consciousness (cit, consciousness; vilācam, radiant display, play). It names the holy hall (citvilācat tiruccapai) of the sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam, which seekers enter by the power of merit. Asked there to tell the holy presence of God's grace as it is, these sages give no word: tears of bliss pour from their holy eyes of great compassion, and they remain still (Gnana §8).

The oneness of Siva-bliss (civāṉantam, the bliss of Sivam, the Auspicious, a name of God; orumai, oneness). By the compassion of His holy heart, God performs the holy dance of this oneness (civāṉanta orumait tirunaṭacceykai), rising full of natural bliss, so that all living beings may attain bliss (Peru §2). See tirunaṭam.

The Space of Siva-experience: the experience of Sivam, the Auspicious, a name of God. Vallalar addresses God as shining in His own form as Arut Perum Jothi, full of natural illumination, in a pure Space of Siva-experience (oru cutta civāṉupava veḷi) filled with natural truth (Peru §2). Compare the great Space of Grace (aruṭperu veḷi, Peru §18) and the Pure Space of Wisdom (cutta ñāṉa veḷi, Siru §3).

Own form, true nature (Skt. svarūpa): what a thing is in itself. The sages say that God, the natural Truth, is Himself all the marks, such as outward form, essential nature and inherent nature, of all things, and that He is also not them; He touches them and is untouched (Gnana §7). The sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam have attained the complete form (pūraṇa corūpam) of the blissful experience of natural true wisdom (Gnana §8). God shines in His own form (corūpar) as Arut Perum Jothi (Peru §2).

The subtle instruments: mind (maṉam), intellect (putti), cittam (the reflecting mind) and the sense of "I" (akaṅkāram), which carry out thinking, considering, deciding and asserting "I". They are among the parts God made appear in the body to serve Vallalar, with the ultra-subtle instruments that set them to work and the qualities (kuṇam), sattva, rajas, tamas and the rest, which serve them as aids (Peru §16). See karaṇam.

Freedom: the power to act by one's own right, and the claim that a thing is one's own. The deathless life is attained only by the freedom of God's holy grace (tiruvaruṭ cutantaram, Sanga §4). It comes where the three freedoms that make up "my I" have gone: the freedom of the body (tēka cutantaram), the freedom of enjoyment (pōka cutantaram) and the freedom of the soul (jīva cutantaram) (Sanga §5). Vallalar gives all three to grace as all freedom (carva cutantaram); God alone has all freedom (carva cutantarar) (Sanga §6).

Suddha Sanmarkkam, the pure true path: the shorter name Vallalar uses within the petitions for his path (see camaraca cutta caṉmārkkam). Its goal is the God of true wisdom (Peru §17); the sects and paths are distinctions of attainment of a slight fraction of its experience (Peru §24); God made Vallalar hold to it alone, the one unique path (cutta caṉmārkkat taṉineṟi, Peru §25). Its chief aim (mukkiya lakṣiyam) is the right of oneness in soul-kinship, and its chief obstacle (mukkiyat taṭai) the religions, sects and paths (Siru §18). Its sages praise God, think of Him, realize Him and unite with Him (Siru §2); its pure sages conquer all the tattvas (Gnana §7).

The Pure Space of Wisdom. All the energies, their agents and all the lords find it exceedingly hard to know, and it shines far, far beyond all the tattvas and all the tattvis. In it God shines as Arut Perum Jothi, unique and supreme, with no equal and none above (Siru §3). Compare the pure Space of Siva-experience (Peru §2) and the great Space of Grace (Peru §18).

Suddha Deham, the pure body: the first of the three bodies, with Pranava Deham (body of the primal sound Om) and Jnana Deham (body of wisdom). Vallalar calls them bodies of the experience of the deathless art (cākāk kalāṉupava tēkaṅkaḷ), which never perish at any time; they belong to the great life of supreme bliss into which God resolved to bring him (Peru §25). See ñāṉatēkam, piraṇavatēkam.

The undivided One. This points to the single source of all existence: despite the vast diversity of life, there is only one supreme God. It is paired with anēkar, the Many, in the invocation (Siru §2).

The One who can do all things, the All-Powerful. It completes a threefold name in the invocation: ellāmāṉavar, the One who is all; ellāmuṭaiyavar, the One who possesses all; and ellām vallavar, the One who can do all (Siru §2). God is addressed by its Sanskrit-derived equal, carva vallapar, the All-Powerful (Peru §2; Siru §17), and again as the One who possesses all (ellāmuṭaiya, Siru §18) and who is all things (ellāmākiya, Siru §19).

Desire, knowledge and action (Skt. icchā, jñāna, kriyā): the soul's three powers. While Vallalar lay in the womb in the physical form of an embryo, God shaped and arranged without any lack, nurtured and protected all the serviceable organs of the tattvas (upayōka tattuva uṟuppukaḷ) needed to aid and to increase the bringing forth of his desire, knowledge and action (Peru §7).

Natural intelligence, natural knowledge: the divine consciousness that knows all things perfectly and effortlessly. God is named Natural Intelligence (iyaṟkai aṟiviṉar, Siru §2). The petitioners speak of their own small knowledge (ciṟṟaṟivu, Siru §2), and of the little knowledge that God made arise in them (ciṟitaṟivu, Siru §4).

Natural bliss: bliss that is God's own nature, uncaused and dependent on nothing. God is named Natural Bliss (iyaṟkai iṉpiṉar, Siru §2) and is the God of natural bliss who is all things (Peru §12). His holy dance of the oneness of Siva-bliss rises full of natural bliss (Peru §2); in the True Hall of Wisdom He performs the true holy dance called natural bliss (Gnana §2). He is the unique great Joy (cukam) of natural bliss, and the pure sages experience natural bliss in natural truth (Gnana §7). Vallalar asks God to grant us all true bliss (uṇmaiyiṉpam, Siru §17).

Natural truth: truth that is God's own nature, not made and not received from anything else. God is named Natural Truth (iyaṟkai uṇmaiyar, Siru §2) and is the God of natural truth who can do all things (Peru §3). The pure Space of Siva-experience in which He shines is filled with natural truth (Peru §2). His true holy form is called natural truth (Gnana §2); He is the unique great Reality (poruḷ) of natural truth, God the natural Truth (Gnana §7); and Vallalar longs to know the natural truth of the holy presence of His grace (Gnana §5).

Natural illumination: light that is God's own nature and shines of itself. God shines in His own form as Arut Perum Jothi, full of natural illumination (Peru §2), and is the God of natural illumination who possesses all (Peru §5). The True Hall of Wisdom, where God has His true holy form and performs His dance, is called natural illumination (Gnana §2); He is the unique great State (patam) of natural illumination (Gnana §7).

Caste. At that young age God made Vallalar know that the false worldly custom (poyyulaka ācāram) called caste custom and life-stage custom (jāti-ācāram, ācirama-ācāram) is false, and kept him from practising them (Peru §22). He prays that worldly customs, notions and distinctions such as varna (caste) and ashrama never take hold of our minds (Siru §18). See ācāram, varuṇam, āciramam.

The individual soul, a living being. The five elements appear in the body to support the soul (jīvaṉ), make it grow, make it shine, increase it and make it pervade (Peru §16). Vallalar's mind does not dare call the compassion of the father, the mother and other living beings (jīvarkaḷ, jīvar) equal to God's: guarding someone for a single moment, they grow weary, grow faint, feel disgust and break off (Peru §12, §13). The great world cannot be measured by living beings (Peru §17).

Return, recompense: what is given back for a kindness received. For God's immense compassion in placing us in this human body, Vallalar confesses that "we know of no recompense at all that we could make" (Siru §11). See maṉita tēkam.

Causal action. Within a single moment God moved Vallalar by causal action into a causal form of primal matter (kāraṇappakuti uru), by ultra-subtle action (aticūkkumak kiriyai) into an ultra-subtle form, by subtle action (cūkkumak kiriyai) into a subtle form, then through the higher and lower energies and their agents into a form of the elements and into the physical form (Peru §15). It follows the supra-causal action (atikāraṇak kiriyai) of Peru §14.

Instrument; especially the inner instruments of knowing (Skt. antaḥkaraṇa): mind, intellect, cittam (the reflecting mind) and the sense of "I". The lords of the five functions do not contemplate God's compassion, holding that their inner instruments have not attained in full the auspicious qualities, such as purity and love; Vallalar calls his own an inner instrument of black stone, the storehouse of all evil qualities (Gnana §3). The inner faculties are among the tattvas the pure sages conquer (Gnana §7). See cūkkumak karaṇam.

Cause. The holy presence of Grace shines as the primary cause (mutaṟkāraṇam, the material, as clay is to a pot), the instrumental cause (nimitta kāraṇam, the maker, as the potter) and the supporting cause (tuṇaik kāraṇam, the aid, as the potter's wheel) of everything, and as none of these (Gnana §9). The energies and their agents run the tattvas by way of cause and effect (kāraṇa kāriyam, Gnana §2).

The good endeavour of compassion. God did not let Vallalar's understanding cling to any desire, for gold, for women, for land, and gave him the good endeavour of compassion, which looks on all living beings alike and longs for all of them to attain bliss; then He made him hold to Suddha Sanmarkkam alone (Peru §25). This is Jeevakarunyam, compassion for all living beings, the foundation of spiritual life. Already in boyhood God led him to compassion for other living beings (piṟavuyirkkiraṅkal, Peru §19).

The human body. God took into His heart the exhaustion, fear, anguish, weariness and sorrow we went through in each of the earlier births, took pity on us, and placed us in "this human body, which has the high intelligence fit for attaining the imperishable great life" (aḻiyāp peruvāḻvu, Siru §11). Vallalar prays also for all others "in this world who have received this body" (Siru §17). In Peru God placed him in this human body, which has six kinds of awareness (Peru §2). Sanga calls it a body of high standing with six kinds of awareness, and asks that this very body be made eternal (Sanga §3).

A deity in embodied form (Skt. mūrti, form). The deities (mūrttikaḷ) and others wished to praise the great glory of the holy presence of God's grace, but stand in fear without praising, because their tongues are not perfected in such disciplines as speaking truth and speaking sweet words (Gnana §4). All divine forms and all who bear them (mūrttar) have the holy presence of Grace as their cause (Gnana §9).

The Hall of Wisdom (Jnana Sabha); also tiruñāṉa capai, the holy Hall of Wisdom. Through an intimation of His grace, God made known that He would perform the dance of grace in Uttara Jnana Siddhipuram, and that a Hall of Wisdom must be established there as its sign; in the form of grace He caused it to arise and shine (Siru §15). The petitioners begin its adornment and ask God to bring that holy service to completion (Siru §16). It is the Sathya Jnana Sabha at Vadalur; see cattiya ñāṉacapai. There God bears His holy form and performs the dance of grace so that every living being may attain bliss (Sanga §2).

Jnana Deham, the body of wisdom: the third of the three bodies, with Suddha Deham (pure body) and Pranava Deham (body of the primal sound Om), which Vallalar calls bodies of the experience of the deathless art (cākāk kalāṉupava tēkaṅkaḷ), never perishing at any time (Peru §25). Those who have it are ñāṉatēkikaḷ: the sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam are eternal ones with bodies pure, of sound and of wisdom (nittiya cutta catta ñāṉatēkikaḷ), which nothing hinders at any time, in any place or in any way (Gnana §8).

A sage, one who has true wisdom (ñāṉam). The sages of Suddha Sanmarkkam (cutta caṉmārkka ñāṉikaḷ) praise God, think of Him, realize Him and unite with Him, and so experience Him (Siru §2). No one can grasp the power of attainment of the true sages (uṇmai ñāṉikaḷ, Gnana §2); Vallalar takes the true saying of the sages of true wisdom (cattiyañāṉikaḷ) as his support (Gnana §5). Asked how the holy presence of God's grace is, the sages of Suddha Sanmarkkam sigh (Gnana §7), and those of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam give no word and remain still (Gnana §8). The opposite is the aññāṉi, the ignorant one (Siru §4).

The class of hellish births, the last before the human body. Vallalar lists dwellers in the wild (kāṭṭakattār), deceivers (karavu ceyvār), killers (kolai ceyvār) and the like. In these "we" died again and again through such afflictions as fear, imprisonment and being broken apart, and wandered through them all until exhausted (Siru §10).

The sound of Nada, the primal sound (Skt. nāda). Whenever the unborn child was afraid, terrified by ghosts (pēy) and by the great darkness, God drove away the terror of ghosts by the sound of Nada and the great darkness by the light of Bindu (vintu viḷakkam), and took away its fear (Peru §9).

The stainless: those free of all impurity (Skt. nirmala). The pure Yogantars, Kalantars, Bodhantars, Nadantars, Vedantars and Siddhantars, sages of Suddha Sanmarkkam, have conquered all the tattvas by the power of God's grace (tiruvaruḷ valam), become stainless (niṉmalarāki) and stand at the end of the tattvas (tattuvāntam). Yet asked how the holy presence of God's grace is, they can only cry, "Alas! Alas!! How shall we know!", and sigh (Gnana §7).

The Unsurpassed One (nir-atiśaya, with nothing surpassing): nothing in all creation surpasses God (Siru §2). Vallalar adds that in no way at all can any equal or any superior to God be pointed to (oppuyarvu, Siru §3).

The One beyond the guṇas: free of the three qualities of nature (purity, passion and lethargy; Skt. sattva, rajas, tamas) that shape every embodied being. It is paired with ciṟkuṇar, the One whose quality is Consciousness (Siru §2). God is untouched by the qualities of matter, and His own nature is knowing. It does not mean "without any attributes": the same invocation names God by many attributes.

The eternal body: this very body, freed from death, disease, old age, fear and suffering and made to last for ever. It is Vallalar's true desire and most intense endeavour (Sanga §3), and he asks for it again after giving up every freedom of his own (Sanga §6). See pēriṉpam.

The Eternal One: God, without beginning or end (Siru §2). Vallalar asks God, by the illumination of His wondrous grace, to make us and all others in this world who have received this body eternal beings (nittiyarkaḷ) who live for ever (Siru §17). The sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam are eternal ones (nittiya) with bodies pure, of sound and of wisdom (Gnana §8).

Bondage (Skt. pāśa, noose, fetter): what binds the soul (pacu). Vallalar speaks of the great darkness called bondage, from which no one could in any way separate him. In it he lay in a swoon, shrunken and mingled with it, with no difference between "I" and "it", for time beyond measure; within a single moment God drew him out of it by supra-causal action (Peru §14). See pācāntakāram.

The darkness of bondage (pācam, bondage; antakāram, darkness). Vallalar calls ignorance (aññāṉam), in which knowledge did not appear even a little, a great darkness of bondage. He lay in it for a long time as a tiny atom-soul, until God, the inner light within him, lifted him out of it and placed him in this human body (Peru §2). Peru §14 calls the same state the great darkness (makāntakāram) called bondage.

Prakriti (Skt. prakṛti): primal matter, the root from which bodies are formed; the translation renders it "primal matter". In the father's seed God set Vallalar in the form of a great atom of primal matter (pakutip pēraṇu) and created that form (Peru §3), and guarded him in it (Peru §12). He drew him out of the darkness of bondage in a supra-causal form of primal matter (Peru §14) and moved him through its causal, ultra-subtle and subtle forms into the elemental and physical forms (Peru §15).

The class of winged births. Vallalar lists flying insects and birds together: flies, beetles, bees, sparrows, crows, kites, eagles and the like. In these "we" died again and again through such afflictions as being beaten, caught, tossed about and tormented, and wandered through them all until exhausted (Siru §7).

Stage of life. Three appear: infancy (cicup paruvam), boyhood (kumārap paruvam) and youth (vālipap paruvam). God guarded Vallalar from infancy until boyhood (Peru §18). In boyhood He led him to good deeds (Peru §19) and trained him without a teacher (Peru §20); at that young age He made known that caste and life-stage customs are false (Peru §22). As youth drew near He held down its desires (Peru §23); before it appeared He made known the one true God, and then the truth about the religions (Peru §24).

The physical form: the body made of the elements (pavutikam, Skt. bhautika, from pūtam, element). God set Vallalar in the womb in the physical form of an embryo (pavutika piṇṭa vaṭivu, Peru §7). The physical form is the last of the forms into which God moved him in a single moment, through the lower energies and their agents (Peru §15); all the parts of the body, inner and outer, appear together within it to serve him (Peru §16).

Supreme bliss. Vallalar longs for the attainment of supreme bliss (pēriṉpa citti) and the great life it brings (pēriṉpa cittip peruvāḻvu), in which one is freed from death, disease, old age, fear and suffering (Siru §13–§15). God resolves to bring him into the great life of supreme bliss (pēriṉpap peruvāḻvu), lived in possession of the deathless bodies, the unique great power that by one's own freedom directs all the tattvas, the true wisdom that knows there is only one God, and the gift of grace by which all attainments are obtained (Peru §25). See aḻiyāp peruvāḻvu. Sanga asks for the same great life, never perishing, in this very body made eternal (Sanga §3, §4, §6).

The great Lord (pati, lord, master). The invocation of Siru ends by calling God taṉittalaimaip perum pati, the Great Lord of unique supremacy (Siru §2). He is taṉipperum pati, the unique great Lord: of natural, unique and great compassion (Gnana §2), Arut Perum Jothi the unique great Lord (Gnana §5, §7), and the unique great Lord of natural truth (Gnana §8). He is also the great Lord of great compassion (peruṅkaruṇaip perumpati, Gnana §9).

Great compassion, immense compassion. The invocation cries out to the God of Great Compassion (peruṅkaruṇaik kaṭavuḷ, Siru §2). God is the unique great Lord of natural, unique and great compassion (Gnana §2) and the great Lord of great compassion (peruṅkaruṇaip perumāṉ, Gnana §4; peruṅkaruṇaip perumpati, Gnana §9); Vallalar longs to contemplate the great compassion of the holy presence of Grace (Gnana §5). In his Great Discourse (Pērupatēcam) Vallalar says that kindness (tayavu), compassion (karuṇai) and grace (aruḷ) all name one and the same thing; that kindness shown to every living being is Jeevakarunyam, the foundation of the path. See tiruvaruṭ peruṅkaruṇai. Body, soul and the things we enjoy were given by God's great compassion (Sanga §6); Sanga ends with salutations to the reign of His great compassion (Sanga §8).

The body; here the body of the unborn child, the embryo. Vallalar lies in the womb in the form of an embryo (piṇṭa vaṭivu, Peru §7–§10). There God relieved its heat and faintness (Peru §8), fed it, took away its fear and made one kind of awareness (ōraṟivu) shine in it (Peru §9), and set in it the good things to be enjoyed after birth (Peru §10). It is the great form of the embryo (piṇṭap peru vaṭivu) that followed the elemental atom (Peru §13). See aṇṭa piṇṭam.

Pranava Deham, the body of the primal sound Om (piraṇavam, Skt. praṇava): the second of the three bodies, with Suddha Deham (pure body) and Jnana Deham (body of wisdom). Vallalar calls them bodies of the experience of the deathless art (cākāk kalāṉupava tēkaṅkaḷ), which never perish at any time (Peru §25). See cuttatēkam, ñāṉatēkam.

The Complete One: the perfect, whole being. God shines everywhere as the Complete One (Siru §13). Vallalar addresses Him as the Complete One, Arut Perum Jothi, the unique great Lord, who fills and shines within and without all things, the universe, the body and all else (Gnana §5). The same word, pūraṇam, complete, describes the full freedom (pūraṇa cutantaram) of the sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam and the complete form of the blissful experience they have attained (Gnana §8).

Element (Skt. bhūta): earth, water, fire, air and space. The five elements, with the secondary elements (upappirutivi, upanīr, upākkiṉi, upavāyu), appear in the body to support, grow, illumine, increase and pervade the soul (jīvaṉ, Peru §16). The body's first form in the womb is the elemental great atom (pūtap pēraṇu, Peru §5, §7, §13); God had the unborn child fed with nectar formed of the elements (Peru §9). "Element" renders pūtam only; the tattvas (tattuvam) are a wider class.

The elemental great atom, the great atom of the elements: the first form of the body in the mother's womb. God joined Vallalar to the mass of blood in the womb and placed him there in this form to grow and come forth; as the inner light within him, God created it (Peru §5). He kept it from being scattered or changed by poisonous germs, air and flame until it became a physical embryo (Peru §7). Compare pakuti (the great atom of primal matter, Peru §3, §12).

Unique supremacy: lordship that stands alone (taṉi, single, without a second). God is addressed as the God of unique supremacy (taṉittalaimaik kaṭavuḷ) who is all-powerful (carva vallapar, Peru §2; Siru §17), who is Arut Perum Jothi (Peru §13), who is true wisdom and bliss (Peru §15), and who is all things and none of them (Peru §20); the invocation of Gnana ends with the same name (Gnana §2). He is the Great Lord of unique supremacy (taṉittalaimaip perum pati, Siru §2). The fuller form taṉipperun talaimai, unique great supremacy, belongs to Arut Perum Jothi (Siru §3, §19).

Tattva (plural tattvas): the constituent principles of which bodies, senses, minds and worlds are made. The five elements (pūtam) are among them; a tattva is not simply an element. The tattvis (tattuvikaḷ) are the beings who preside over them (Siru §3; Gnana §8). Hostile tattvas did not hinder Vallalar's form in the seed and the womb (Peru §3, §5). The religions, with their practices, gods and goals, are varieties of attainment within the tattvas (Peru §24); the great life of supreme bliss includes the power to direct all the tattvas by one's own freedom (Peru §25). The Pure Space of Wisdom shines far beyond them (Siru §3); the pure sages conquer them and stand at their end (tattuvāntam, Gnana §7).

The class of stationary births: the first births after we left the darkness of ignorance. Vallalar lists grass, paddy, trees, bushes and herbs, and stones, mountains and hills. In these "we" died again and again through such afflictions as being weeded out, chopped down, reaped, plucked, dried out, shattered and blasted, and wandered through them all until exhausted (Siru §5).

Kindness, compassion. God is the God whose compassion surpasses even a mother's (tāyiṉuñ ciṟanta tayavuṭaik kaṭavuḷ, Siru §4). He guarded Vallalar in the womb with great kindness (peruntayavu, Peru §13), and now, dwelling in his inmost heart and mingled with his life, in great kindness performs the holy dance there (Peru §25). In his Great Discourse (Pērupatēcam) Vallalar says that tayavu, karuṇai (compassion) and aruḷ (grace) all name one and the same thing. The same kindness shown to every living being is Jeevakarunyam, the foundation of the path.

The southern language: Tamil. God turned Vallalar's desire away from Āriyam (Sanskrit) and the other such languages and made his mind hold to the southern language alone, which came to him by the strength of God's holy grace (tiruvaruḷ valam). It is very easy to learn and to know, very sweet to sing and to praise in, and makes known with ease the learning of deathlessness (cākākkalvi); in it God made him sing hymns of praise of many kinds (Peru §21).

You, in the most reverent form. Vallalar addresses God by this honorific throughout the four petitions (Siru §2–§19; Peru §2–§25; Gnana §2–§10; Sanga §2–§8), and it is rendered "You" with a capital. Each work is spoken to God directly: Siru in the plural, "we" (yāṅkaḷ); Peru, Gnana and Sanga in the first person singular, where Vallalar calls himself "Your servant" (aṭiyēṉ, Peru §2, §8) and the smallest of the small (ciṟiyariṟ ciṟiyēṉ, Gnana §3).

The class of deva births. Vallalar lists ghouls (pacācar, pisachas), goblins (pūtar, bhutas), demons (irākkatar, rakshasas), titans (acurar, asuras), gods (curar, suras) and the like. Tēva here names these beings; it does not mean God. In these births too "we" died again and again through such afflictions as being tossed about, acting with arrogance, remaining in forgetfulness, becoming deluded, fighting and being killed, and wandered through them all until exhausted (Siru §9).

Tiruchitrambalam, the holy small hall: the hall of the sacred dance at Chidambaram, also read as cit-ambalam, the hall of consciousness. It stands with the title of each of the four petitions and closes each of them (Siru §1, §19; Peru §1, §25; Gnana §1, §10; Sanga §1, §8).

Sacred indication, sacred sign: a designation that points to God. Through these and other sacred indications and sacred words beyond all measure (aḷavu kaṭanta tirukkuṟipput tiruvārttaikaḷ), the sages of Suddha Sanmarkkam praise, think of, realize, unite with and experience God (Siru §2). The same word returns in tiruvaruṭkuṟippu, the intimation of grace by which God made known His dance of grace and the Hall of Wisdom as its sign (Siru §15); the adornment of the Hall begins "as You indicated" (kuṟippitta vaṇṇam, Siru §16).

The holy dance. By the compassion of His holy heart, God performs the holy dance of the oneness of Siva-bliss (civāṉanta orumait tirunaṭacceykai) so that all living beings may attain bliss (Peru §2). At the close, God dwells in Vallalar's inmost heart, mingles with his life (uyir), and in great kindness (peruntayavāl) performs the holy dance there (Peru §25). In the True Hall of Wisdom He performs the true holy dance called natural bliss (Gnana §2). See aruḷ naṭam.

Sacred word, holy word. With the sacred indications (tirukkuṟippu), these sacred words beyond all measure are the means by which the sages of Suddha Sanmarkkam praise God and come to experience Him (Siru §2). Asked to grant a holy word on the holy presence of Grace as it is, the sages of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam give no holy word, and remain still (Gnana §8).

Divine grace, holy grace. To take even faults as virtues is natural to the greatness of God's grace (Siru §4); in His compassion He took Vallalar's false words as true words (Gnana §3). By His grace the petitioners were made truly to know the one true God, and by the illumination of that grace (tiruvaruḷ viḷakkam) one can be freed from death and the other afflictions (Siru §13, §14). By the strength of His grace (tiruvaruḷ valam) Tamil came to Vallalar (Peru §21), and by its power the pure sages conquer all the tattvas (Gnana §7). See tiruvaruṭ camukam.

The holy presence of Grace (camukam, presence, Skt. sammukha, face to face; not camūkam, assembly), rendered "the holy presence of Your grace" where Vallalar speaks to God. The petitioners make their small petitions in it (Siru §2). It is the subject of the whole of Gnana: Vallalar longs to know its natural truth, contemplate its great compassion and praise its great glory (Gnana §5), yet the sages cannot say how it is (Gnana §7, §8). It is the primary, instrumental and supporting cause of all things, and none of these (Gnana §9); in the end it cannot be known, contemplated or praised in any way (Gnana §10). Vallalar makes the fourth petition in it (Sanga §2).

The great power of (Your) holy grace, the second refrain of Peru. Vallalar asks how he can contemplate and praise it after three works: within a single moment God drew him out of the great darkness of bondage (Peru §14); He moved him through the causal, ultra-subtle and subtle forms into the elemental and physical forms, moving him without moving him (Peru §15); and, standing within, He made all the parts of the body appear to serve him, while He Himself did not appear (Peru §16). See tiruvaruṭ peruṅkaruṇai.

The great compassion of (Your) holy grace: the refrain of Peru. Vallalar asks again and again how he can know, contemplate, speak of and praise it (Peru §2, §4, §11–§13, §25); in Peru §17–§19 it is the great compassion of Your great grace (pēraruṭ peruṅkaruṇai). His mind does not dare call the compassion of father, mother and other living beings equal to it: they weary and break off in guarding even for a moment (Peru §12, §13). Siru closes with salutations to it (Siru §19). See peruṅkaruṇai, tiruvaruṭ pērāṟṟal.

Praising, thinking, realizing, uniting. These are the four ways by which the sages of Suddha Sanmarkkam come to experience (aṉupavikka) God (Siru §2). They praise Him, hold Him in thought, know Him directly, and unite with Him. God shines so that through these four they may experience Him.

The inner light. While Vallalar lay as a tiny atom-soul in the darkness of bondage, God was the inner light within him; He lifted him out and placed him in this human body (Peru §2). Again as the inner light within him, God created the atomic form of primal matter in the father's seed (Peru §3) and the elemental atomic form in the mother's womb (Peru §5).

The true God; in full, ōr uṇmaik kaṭavuḷ, the one true God. By God's grace the petitioners were made truly to know that there is one true God, who shines everywhere as the Complete One (pūraṇar); who brings into being all universes, worlds, living beings and things, makes them shine, removes their impurity, brings them to ripeness and grants them their fruit; and whose grace will appear and shine in our minds if we hold Him in our thought with true love and worship Him (Siru §13). Before youth appeared, God made Vallalar know that there is only one true God, Arut Perum Jothi (Peru §24).

True love. By God's grace the petitioners were made to know that if we hold God in our thought with true love and worship Him, His grace will appear and shine in our minds (Siru §13). See uṇmaik kaṭavuḷ.

Courtesy of speech: calling a thing by a name it does not strictly deserve. Vallalar speaks of "a man called father, who begot me only by courtesy of speech" (upacārattāṟ peṟṟa tantai eṉpāṉ, Peru §3) and of "a woman called mother" in the same words (Peru §4): father and mother only in a manner of speaking. Because his mind does not dare call their compassion equal to the great compassion of God's grace, he will not say so even as a courtesy (upacariyātavaṉāki irukkiṉṟēṉ, Peru §12, §13).

Right; rightful belonging. Gnana ends with it: as far as a servant (aṭimai) is able, knowing without knowing, contemplating without contemplating and praising without praising, Vallalar has made firm his right (eṉatu urimaiyai ūṟṟañ ceykiṉṟavaṉāṉēṉ, Gnana §10). The same word ends āṉmanēya orumaippāṭṭurimai, the right of oneness in soul-kinship (Siru §18). Sanga asks God to make every living being a holder of the same right (Sanga §7).

The class of crawling and water-dwelling births. Vallalar lists ants, termites, worms, snakes, monitor lizards and wall lizards, and frogs, small fish, crocodiles, sharks and whales. In these "we" died again and again through such afflictions as being scraped away, crushed, beaten and caught, and wandered through them all until exhausted (Siru §6).

Uttara Jnana Siddhipuram, the city of the attainment (siddhi) of wisdom. Uttara means both "northern" and "later"; the name is set against pūrvañāṉa citamparam, the ancient (pūrva, "former") Jnana Chidambaram, that is, Chidambaram. It is the place called Parvatipuram, that is, Vadalur, north of Chidambaram; Vallalar elsewhere calls it Uttara Jnana Chidambaram. There God will perform the dance of grace for an immeasurably long time, so that every siddhi shines forth, and a Hall of Wisdom stands there as its sign (Siru §15). Sanga gives all four names together: Uttara Jnana Siddhipuram and Uttara Jnana Chidambaram, made by grace, and Parvatipuram and Vadalur, by which the world marks the place (Sanga §2).

Form, manner: the way a thing is (literally "colour"). The sages of true wisdom declare that Arut Perum Jothi has all forms: the forms that knowers know, contemplators contemplate and praisers praise (Gnana §5); Peru likewise calls Him the One who has every form that knowers know (Peru §19). Yet none of the forms once within reach of Vallalar's knowing, thought and tongue now appears fitting, and he marvels at the natural forms of the holy presence of God's grace (Gnana §6). Tiruvaṇṇam is sacred form (Gnana §9, §10).

Varna: the fourfold division of people by birth into castes (brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, shudra). Vallalar names varna, ashrama and the like as worldly custom (ulakācāram), and asks God that these worldly customs, notions and distinctions (caṅkaṟpa vikaṟpam) never take hold of our minds, from now on and for all time (Siru §18). God made him know, at a young age, that caste custom and life-stage custom are false worldly custom (poyyulaka ācāram), and kept him from practising them (Peru §22).

The Vedas and the Agamas. Even the Vedas and Agamas laid down by those of true knowledge find no words of great worth (peruntakai vācakam) for God's unique greatness; they find only words of small worth (ciṟutakai vācakam), and they stand bewildered (Siru §3). All the Vedas and Agamas set out to know and praise the power of attainment of the true sages; finding no end to it, they embellish their words and marvel (Gnana §2). Vallalar calls the Vedas, Agamas, Puranas, Sastras and the rest of the religions imagined lore of attainment within the tattvas (tattuva cittik kaṟpaṉaik kalaikaḷ, Peru §24).

The class of animal births. Vallalar lists squirrels, monkeys, dogs, pigs, cats, goats, cattle, elephants, horses, tigers and bears. In these "we" died again and again through such afflictions as being caught, beaten, stabbed, slashed, attacked, tied up and struck, and wandered through them all until exhausted (Siru §8). This shared history of suffering is a plain ground for Jeevakarunyam, compassion for all living beings, which Vallalar teaches as the foundation of spiritual life.

A petition: a humble request laid before One far greater. The four works of this volume, numbered 1 to 4 in their Tamil titles, are Vallalar's four prose petitions: the Small True Petition (cattiyac ciṟu viṇṇappam; ciṟu, small, Siru §1), the Great True Petition (cattiyap peru viṇṇappam; peru, great, Peru §1), the True Petition of Wisdom (cattiya ñāṉa viṇṇappam, Gnana §1) and the True Petition of the Sangam (caṅka cattiya viṇṇappam, Sanga §1). Siru speaks in the plural: smaller than a straw, the petitioners make small petitions with small knowledge (Siru §2), and ask God not to mark their faults (Siru §3, §4). Peru, Gnana and Sanga speak as "I". In Gnana the same verb names the request put to the sages (Gnana §7, §8).

The light of Bindu (Skt. bindu), the primal light, paired with Nada, the primal sound. When the unborn child was terrified by the great darkness in the womb, God drove away that darkness by the light of Bindu, as He drove away the terror of ghosts by the sound of Nada (nāta oli), and so took away its fear (Peru §9).

Class (or category) of births; literally, class of wombs. Vallalar names six classes through which "we" passed: stationary (tāvara), crawling and water-dwelling (ūrvaṉa nīr vāḻvaṉa), winged (paṟavai), animal (vilaṅku), deva (tēva) and hellish (naraka) (Siru §5–§10). Each ends with the same refrain: born again and again, dying again and again through many afflictions, wandering through them all until exhausted. Then God took pity on us and placed us in this human body (Siru §11).
